desc:
You are given an array arr of non-negative integers and a list of queries. Each query is a pair [l, r] (0-indexed, both ends inclusive). For every query, compute the bitwise XOR of arr[l], arr[l+1], ..., arr[r].

Return the answers in the order of the queries.

arr = [1, 3, 4, 8], queries = [[0, 1], [1, 2], [0, 3], [3, 3]]
answers: 1^3 = 2,  3^4 = 7,  1^3^4^8 = 14,  8
result = [2, 7, 14, 8]
hints: Answering each query by looping from l to r is O(n) per query. Can the work be shared between queries?
Just as range sums use prefix sums, think about a prefix XOR: px[i] is the XOR of the first i elements.
Since x ^ x = 0, px[r+1] ^ px[l] cancels the common prefix and leaves exactly the XOR of arr[l..r].
editorial: XOR is associative and every value is its own inverse, so it plays the same role that addition and subtraction play for sums. Let px[0] = 0 and px[i+1] = px[i] ^ arr[i]. Then px[r+1] is the XOR of arr[0..r] and px[l] is the XOR of arr[0..l-1]; XOR-ing them cancels the first l elements and leaves arr[l..r].

Build the prefix array once in O(n) and answer each query with one XOR in O(1). Total time O(n + q), extra space O(n). The idea is the base of every XOR-with-prefix trick: two equal prefix values mean the block between them has XOR 0.
